screens.prompt: In B5, look up the month in B4 across the top row of B1:D3 and write that month's price.

hints.syntax: =HLOOKUP(B4,B1:D3,3,FALSE): the answer row is the third one down from the month header.
hints.func-hlookup: HLOOKUP reads across a row. VLOOKUP would search column B for a month and find none.
hints.match-type: FALSE as the fourth argument. Calendar order is not alphabetical order, so a near miss would be allowed to stop on the wrong month.
hints.require-ref: Take the month from B4, so the price answers the cell rather than a typed word.
hints.value: That is the units figure. Row 3 of B1:D3 holds the price, so the third argument is 3.
hints.error: B1:D3 is three rows deep, so the third argument has to be 1, 2 or 3, and a number. #VALUE! comes from the word price in that slot.

reject.why: no fourth argument means approximate match, but the exercise wants an exact one written
approximate match is free to stop on a neighbouring month
VLOOKUP searches column B for the month and finds nothing
the month is typed in, so the answer never follows B4
row 2 holds units, so this returns 180
a text row number stops the formula with #VALUE!

docs.explain:
HLOOKUP runs across the first row until it meets the month, then drops to the row number you name. The table B1:D3 has months in row 1, units in row 2 and prices in row 3. Feb sits in column C, so the third row there holds 5.

The row number is the trap. A 2 would return 180, the units figure, and it would pass as a price until someone checked it against the sheet. Count rows from the top of the range rather than the top of the sheet.

Write FALSE for an exact match. These headers run in calendar order, not alphabetical order. Approximate match assumes the top row is sorted, so a near miss can settle on the neighbouring month.

errors.text: The month is not in the first row of B1:D3, so there is no column to read down.
The row number is the word price rather than a number.
The row number reaches below row 3 of B1:D3, so the answer sits outside the range.

docs.atWork: Shift rosters and price sheets with the months across the top, read sideways.
docs.outcome: Pull a price out of a row table by naming the row it sits on.

seo.title: HLOOKUP in Excel: read across a row table
seo.description: HLOOKUP finds a month in the first row and reads down to the row you name. Row 3 holds the price, so a 2 would quietly return the units figure instead.
